newsitem.title: USA: U.S. balloonist may end flight in India.
newsitem.headline: U.S. balloonist may end flight in India.

text.p: U.S. balloonist Steve Fossett's record-breaking voyage was set to end well short of his around-the-world goal on Sunday as his team tried to calculate the best landing spot.

The commodity broker-turned-adventurer, said to be tired and cold as he passed over India, was hoping to break the six-day and 16-minute endurance record for a balloon flight later on Sunday while finding somewhere safe to put down.
Projections by his support team in Chigaco suggest Fossett will land near Calcutta or possibly 100 miles to 200 miles (160-320 km) beyond in Bangladesh later in the day.
"That would take him nearly half-way around the world," said Doug Blount, a member of the tracking team at mission control headquarters at Chicago's Loyola University.
That would enable Fossett to beat the endurance record set in 1981 by Americans Ben Abruzzo and Troy Bradley.
"He could go several more days and put down in the middle of the Pacific (Ocean), but I don't think that's in the cards," Blount said.

Fossett, who took off from Busch Stadium in St. Louis. on Monday, broke his own record for balloon distance travel when he passed 5,435 miles (8,747 km) over Algeria on Friday. He set the earlier mark on a voyage from South Korea to Canada.
Electronic communication between Fossett and his ground team has been sparse, but Blount said the 52-year-old was "tired and cold."
Opportunities for sleep were sporadic, and temperatures have hovered around 15 degrees (-10 Celsius).
At 0744 EST (1244 GMT), Fossett was eastbound over central India under favourable winds propelling him at 138 mph (222 kph). His altitude was about 23,000 feet (7,000 metres).
Blount said travelling beyond Bangladesh would bring Fossett's 150-foot (45 metre) double-skinned balloon over south China, where flying permission remained unresolved.
Earlier in the journey, political turbulence over the use of Lybian air space cost Fossett his around-the-world bid.

Although Libya later relented and Fossett's "Solo Spirit" cut across the southeastern tip of the country, his forced change of route cost him fuel he planned on using to cross the Pacific back to the United States, as well as putting him in a slower wind pattern.
